My grandmother kept a list on the refrigerator of things people had borrowed. When somebody returned something, she drew a line through it but left it on the list. By the time my mother and I came to empty her apartment, nearly everything had a line through it. Three entries remained:

Dean — six folding chairs  
Ruth — blue suitcase  
Calvin — the good ladder

“We haven’t got room for six folding chairs,” my mother said.

She was on the kitchen floor, trying to separate two roasting pans that had spent several decades becoming one roasting pan. I put the list in my pocket. It gave me something to do besides decide which of my grandmother’s possessions deserved to survive her, a job for which I had discovered I was both unqualified and, in my mother’s opinion, too slow.

Dean lived downstairs. He opened the door in his socks and listened while I explained about the chairs.

“Well, where shall we start?” he said.

I thought this was a peculiar answer. Then he showed me.

One chair was by his front door so he could sit to put his shoes on. Two stood at the kitchen table. A fourth held a geranium in the sunny bit of the bedroom. The fifth was in the hall cupboard, and the sixth was with a man named Paul who played the accordion at the Saturday farmers’ market.

“Does he sit on it to play?”

“No, he puts the case on it. Bad back. People throw money in.”

I told Dean I wasn’t there to collect the chairs. This hadn’t been entirely true when I rang his bell, but it was by the time I left.

Ruth had moved to Manitoba. Her sister gave me a phone number and warned me about the time difference, which I got wrong in the other direction and ended up calling her during lunch.

“Oh, that suitcase,” Ruth said. “Has she told you what happened?”

I sat on the bare floor where my grandmother’s bed had been. There was a pale rectangle on the wallpaper and, at shoulder height, a little brown teardrop where she used to lean her head to read.

Ruth had borrowed the suitcase for a train trip. On the way home, one of the catches sprang open and her underwear fell out in the dining car. A boy of about eight calmly picked up a pair of her underpants with the salad tongs.

“He was trying to be polite,” Ruth said. “That was the worst of it. You couldn’t get cross with him.”

She’d bought a strap to hold the suitcase shut. My grandmother had refused to take it back.

“She said it had learned to travel and it would be a shame to stop it now.”

“Did she really say that?”

“No. She said, ‘What do I want with a busted suitcase?’ But I’ve told the story a few times.”

Calvin, it turned out, was dead. His son answered the phone.

“Aluminum ladder? Red paint on the bottom step?”

I said I didn’t know.

“Creaks on the third rung?”

Again, I didn’t know.

He seemed reluctant to let me claim a ladder on the strength of such inadequate credentials. I explained that my grandmother had died too, that nobody wanted the ladder, that I was just going down a list.

“Oh,” he said. “I’ve got one of those.”

I asked what was on it.

“A guy named Dean has Dad’s socket set.”

Downstairs, Dean received this news without enthusiasm.

“He owed me forty dollars,” he said.

“Well, he’s dead.”

“That’s going to complicate things.”

He looked in the hall cupboard, behind the fifth chair. No socket set. We tried the bedroom closet and the cabinet under the sink. Finally he remembered he’d given it to my grandmother, whose kitchen tap once made a hammering noise so loud you could hear it in his apartment.

Upstairs, my mother had progressed to the drawer beneath the oven. She had found seventeen baking sheets and was furious with all of them. I opened the cabinet under the sink. Behind a bottle of ammonia and a paper bag full of paper bags was a green tin box.

Every socket was there. There was also a piece of masking tape inside the lid, in my grandmother’s handwriting:

Calvin’s. Dean owes him an apology.

I read this to Dean over the phone.

“That’s her interpretation,” he said.

Calvin’s son came that evening. He brought the ladder despite my protests, because it had been on his truck for three days and he wanted the space. My mother, who by then had remembered the light fixture in the hall, unfolded it without a word.

When she stepped on the third rung, it creaked.

“There you go,” I said to Calvin’s son.

He smiled for the first time. Then he held the ladder steady while my mother unscrewed the glass shade and tipped thirty years of dead moths into my cupped hands.
